title: Periclymenus
titleEn: Nestor's Grudge and the Death of Periclymenus — Metamorphoses XII.536–579
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Tlepolemus breaks in on Nestor's account of the Lapiths and the Centaurs to protest that his father Hercules has been left out of it, and Nestor answers with the walls he threw down at Messene and the cities of Elis and Pylos, and with the eleven brothers he lost. Among them was Periclymenus, to whom Neptune had given the power to take any shape he wished and lay it aside again, and who was shot down in the form of the bird that carries Jupiter's thunderbolts.

sentences.t:
Haec inter Lapithas et semihomines Centauros
proelia Tlepolemus Pylio referente dolorem
praeteriti Alcidae tacito non pertulit ore
atque ait:
sentences.l: While the Pylian was recounting these battles between the Lapiths and the half-human Centaurs, Tlepolemus did not endure with silent mouth his grief at Alcides passed over, and says:
sentences.i: While the man of Pylos was telling of these battles between the Lapiths and the half-human Centaurs, Tlepolemus could not keep his mouth shut on his resentment at Hercules being passed over, and said:
sentences.n: Pylio referente is an ablative absolute with haec ... proelia as its object, “with the Pylian recounting them”; the Pylian is Nestor, and Ovid is narrating here. Alcides is Hercules, named from Alceus, his father's father. praeteriti agrees with Alcidae, and the whole genitive depends on dolorem: grief at Hercules passed over — passed over, that is, in the telling. tacito ... ore is an ablative of manner, its adjective and noun separated by non pertulit.

sentences.t:
“Herculeae mirum est oblivia laudis
acta tibi, senior!
sentences.l: “Astonishing it is that forgettings of Herculean glory have been performed by you, old man!
sentences.i: “It is astonishing that you should have let Hercules' glory slip your mind, old man!
sentences.n: mirum est governs an accusative-and-infinitive with esse left out: oblivia ... acta [esse] tibi, “that forgettings have been performed by you”. tibi is a dative of agent, the regular agent with a perfect passive participle. oblivia is a neuter plural for the single act of forgetting, and Herculeae is separated from its noun laudis by the whole of mirum est oblivia. senior, the comparative of senex, is plain address, “the older man”; the speaker is Tlepolemus, and at 573–574 Nestor names his father for him, tui ... Herculis.

sentences.t:
Certe mihi saepe referre
nubigenas domitos a se pater esse solebat.”
sentences.l: Certainly my father used often to relate to me that the cloud-born ones had been tamed by him.”
sentences.i: My father, at any rate, used to tell me time and again that he himself had tamed the cloud-born.”
sentences.n: nubigenas, “cloud-born”, is the Centaurs: their mother was a cloud. The accusative-and-infinitive nubigenas domitos [esse] a se depends on referre, which is itself the infinitive after solebat. a se is reflexive and points back to pater, the subject of solebat — Hercules, whom Tlepolemus is here claiming as his father.

sentences.t:
Tristis ad haec Pylius: “Quid me meminisse malorum
cogis et obductos oculis rescindere luctus
inque tuum genitorem odium offensasque fateri?
sentences.l: The Pylian, grieving, in answer to this: “Why do you force me to remember evils, and to tear open again griefs drawn over before my eyes, and to confess hatred and resentments against your father?
sentences.i: Grim at that, the man of Pylos: “Why do you force me to call up old wrongs, to cut open a grief that had closed over, and to own to the hatred and the resentment I bear your father?
sentences.n: The verb of speaking is left out — Tristis ad haec Pylius, “Grieving, at this, the Pylian” — and the quotation supplies it; tristis is nominative, describing Nestor as he answers. Quid is “why”, and cogis governs three infinitives in turn: meminisse (perfect in form, present in meaning), rescindere, and the deponent fateri. rescindere is the surgeon's word for cutting a closed wound open again, and obductos is what a wound does in skinning over. Magnus prints oculis, which is not easy to construe: the griefs are drawn over and so screened from the eyes. Some editions print annis, “by the years”, where the healing is plainly time's work. inque is et in, and in tuum genitorem governs both nouns: the odium and the offensae alike are aimed at Hercules, not committed by him — offensae here are the offences taken, the standing grievances.

sentences.t:
Ille quidem maiora fide, di! gessit et orbem
inplevit meritis, quod mallem posse negare:
sentences.l: He indeed performed things greater than belief — gods! — and filled the world with his deserts, which I would rather be able to deny:
sentences.i: He did, I grant, things past believing — you gods! — and filled the world with what he had earned; and I would rather be in a position to deny it:
sentences.n: maiora fide is “greater than trust”, with fide an ablative of comparison: deeds past believing. di! is a bare vocative exclamation dropped into the middle of the sentence, between fide and gessit. merita are services that earn a return, so orbem inplevit meritis is the world filled with what he is owed for. quod is a connecting relative picking up the whole admission just made, and mallem is a potential imperfect subjunctive, “I would rather” — a wish Nestor knows will not be granted. The concession is grudging by construction: quidem grants it and the relative clause takes it back.

sentences.t:
sed neque Deiphobum nec Polydamanta nec ipsum
Hectora laudamus—quis enim laudaverit hostem?
sentences.l: but neither Deiphobus nor Polydamas nor Hector himself do we praise — for who would praise an enemy?
sentences.n: Polydamanta and Hectora carry Greek accusative singulars in -a, the endings Ovid keeps for Greek names; Deiphobum has the ordinary Latin one. laudaverit is a potential perfect subjunctive, “who would praise?”, not a future perfect. All three named men are Trojans, the enemy side, and that is the whole of Nestor's argument: Hercules stands to him as those three stand to the Greeks. The dash is Magnus's own punctuation, and he prints it without spaces.

sentences.t:
Ille tuus genitor Messenia moenia quondam
stravit et inmeritas urbes Elimque Pylumque
diruit inque meos ferrum flammamque penatis
inpulit,
sentences.l: That father of yours once laid low the Messenian walls, and razed undeserving cities, Elis and Pylos both, and drove sword and flame into my household gods,
sentences.i: That father of yours once flattened the walls of Messene, tore down cities that had done nothing to deserve it — Elis and Pylos both — and drove fire and sword into my own hearth,
sentences.n: Ille tuus genitor, “that father of yours”, is contemptuous, and Nestor still does not use the name. stravit, diruit and inpulit are three perfects sharing one subject, each with its own object. inmeritas, “undeserving”, is Nestor's verdict on the cities and not a neutral epithet. penatis is the accusative plural in -is, the older form beside -es: the Penates are the household gods, so ferrum flammamque in penatis is fire and sword carried into the home itself. inque is again et in.

sentences.t:
utque alios taceam, quos ille peremit,
bis sex Nelidae fuimus, conspecta iuventus:
sentences.l: and — that I may say nothing of the others whom he destroyed — we sons of Neleus were twice six, a much-looked-at body of young men:
sentences.i: and, to pass over the others he killed, there were twelve of us, Neleus' sons, young men everybody looked at:
sentences.n: ut ... taceam is a subjunctive used as an aside, “that I may say nothing of”, with the relative clause quos ille peremit inside it. bis sex, “twice six”, is the poetic way of saying twelve. Nelidae are the sons of Neleus, Nestor's own brothers: he is counting his family. conspecta iuventus stands in apposition to the “we” of fuimus — iuventus is a collective, a body of young men, and conspecta is “looked at”, hence conspicuous.

sentences.t:
bis sex Herculeis ceciderunt me minus uno
viribus;
sentences.l: twice six fell to Herculean strength, less by one, me;
sentences.i: the twelve fell to Hercules' strength — all of them but me;
sentences.n: bis sex opens 553 and 554 alike: the same twelve counted first alive and then dead. me minus uno is “one fewer, and that one me”, so eleven of the twelve fell and Nestor is the survivor. Herculeis stands in 554 and its noun viribus opens 555, adjective and noun split across the line-end; vires is the plural noun of bodily strength, so what killed them is named as force, not as glory.

sentences.t: atque alios vinci potuisse ferendum est:
sentences.l: and that others could be conquered is a thing to be borne:
sentences.i: and that others could be beaten, a man can put up with:
sentences.n: The accusative-and-infinitive alios vinci potuisse is itself the subject of ferendum est: “that others were able to be conquered is to be endured”. vinci is a present passive infinitive and potuisse a perfect active one, so the literal string is “to have been able to be conquered”. ferendum est is the gerundive of obligation, used here of what a man can fairly be asked to bear.

sentences.t:
mira Periclymeni mors est, cui posse figuras
sumere, quas vellet, rursusque reponere sumptas
Neptunus dederat, Nelei sanguinis auctor.
sentences.l: astonishing is the death of Periclymenus, to whom Neptune, the begetter of the Nelean blood, had given the power to take on shapes, whichever ones he might wish, and to put back again the ones taken on.
sentences.i: it is the death of Periclymenus that is astonishing: Neptune, from whom the line of Neleus came, had granted him the power to take on whatever shape he wanted and to lay the taken shape aside again.
sentences.n: The gift is put as a bare infinitive: dederat cui posse, “had given him to be able”, with posse as the thing given. figuras sumere and reponere sumptas are the two halves of the power, taking a shape on and putting it off, and sumptas is the perfect participle of that same verb, “the ones already taken on”, so the second infinitive exactly undoes the first. quas vellet is subjunctive because the choosing is inside the terms of the gift and repeatable, “whichever he might want”. Nelei sanguinis auctor makes Neptune the origin of Neleus' line, which is Nestor's own line: Periclymenus is one of the twelve brothers just counted.

sentences.l: He, when he had varied himself to no purpose into all shapes, turns into the form of the bird which is accustomed to carry thunderbolts in its curved feet, most pleasing to the king of the gods;
sentences.i: When shifting through every shape had got him nowhere, he turned into the shape of the bird that carries the thunderbolt in its hooked feet, the bird the king of the gods likes best;
sentences.n: variatus est is passive in form but reflexive in force — he varied himself — and vertitur does the same work again, “turns himself into”. ubi with the perfect indicative is the “when” of a completed act. The bird is never named: it is identified by what it does, carry the thunderbolts, which makes it the eagle. gratissima is feminine because volucris is, and regi divum is the dative after it; divum is the shortened poetic genitive plural for divorum, “of the gods”.

sentences.t:
Viribus usus avis pennis rostroque redunco
hamatisque viri laniaverat unguibus ora:
sentences.l: Having used a bird's strength, with wings and hooked beak and barbed claws he had mangled the man's face:
sentences.i: Using a bird's strength, he had torn the man's face with wings, hooked beak and barbed talons:
sentences.n: usus is the perfect participle of the deponent utor, active in meaning, “having used”, and it takes the ablative viribus. avis is most naturally genitive with viribus, “of a bird”, though the same form could be nominative in apposition to the subject, “he, now a bird”. Three ablatives of means pile up with -que ... -que: pennis, rostro redunco, unguibus hamatis. ora is a poetic plural for the one face, and viri, “of the man”, is Hercules. laniaverat is pluperfect: the mauling is already done before the shot that follows. Magnus prints Viribus with a capital after the semicolon at the end of 561, where elsewhere in these lines he prints a small letter after a semicolon (atque at 555, nec at 567). The capital may be a stray of the kind this archive carries, or it may mean Magnus took a new sentence to begin here; the text is left exactly as printed either way.

sentences.l: the Tirynthian draws against him his all-too-unerring bow, and strikes him as he carries his limbs high among the clouds and hangs there, where the wing is joined to the side;
sentences.i: the man of Tiryns bends his bow on him — a bow far too accurate — and hits him as he holds himself up among the clouds and hangs there, right at the join of wing and side;
sentences.n: Tirynthius, “the man of Tiryns”, is Hercules, named from the city; Nestor names him by place rather than by name. arcus is a fourth-declension accusative plural used for the one bow, and nimium certos, “all too unerring”, is Nestor's judgement on it, not a compliment. ferentem and pendentem are present participles used as the object of ferit, and they refer to the same man as hunc, which is governed by in after tendit: he is struck in the act of holding himself aloft. qua is the adverb “where”, and lateri is dative after iungitur. Magnus prints hunc, masculine, so the target is named as Periclymenus the man; some editions print hanc, feminine, which makes it the bird he has become.

sentences.t:
nec grave vulnus erat sed rupti vulnere nervi
deficiunt motumque negant viresque volandi.
sentences.l: nor was the wound a heavy one, but the sinews, burst by the wound, fail and refuse motion and the strength of flying.
sentences.i: The wound was not a bad one, but the sinews it burst give way and deny him movement and the power of flight.
sentences.n: The tense shifts under the reader: erat is imperfect, then deficiunt and negant are present, the vivid present for the moment of collapse. rupti agrees with nervi and vulnere is an ablative of means, so the same wound called not heavy is the one that bursts them — that contrast is the point of the sentence. volandi is a genitive gerund, “of flying”, depending on vires.

sentences.t:
Decidit in terram, non concipientibus auras
infirmis pennis, et qua levis haeserat alae,
corporis adfixi pressa est gravitate sagitta
perque latus summum iugulo est exacta sinistro.
sentences.l: He falls down to earth, his weak wings not catching the air, and where the light arrow had lodged in the wing, it was pressed by the weight of the fastened body and driven out through the top of the side at the left throat.
sentences.i: He drops to the ground, the useless wings taking no hold on the air; and at the point in the wing where the light shaft had lodged, it was pressed home by the weight of the body pinned on it, and driven through the upper flank to come out at the left of the throat.
sentences.n: non concipientibus auras infirmis pennis is an ablative absolute, “the weak wings not taking in the air”; concipere is used of taking something in and keeping hold of it. In qua levis haeserat alae the subject sagitta is held back to the next line, and levis is nominative agreeing with it — the light shaft, set against gravitate, the weight of the fastened body, corporis adfixi, which is what drives it home. (Some would take levis with alae, “of the light wing”; the contrast with the body's weight stands either way.) haeserat takes the dative alae. exacta est is “was driven out”, and the shaft travels through latus summum, the top of the flank, to emerge at the left of the throat. Magnus prints adfixi, the body fastened on the shaft; some editions print adflicti, the body dashed down.

sentences.t:
Nunc videor debere tui praeconia rebus
Herculis, o Rhodiae rector pulcherrime classis?
sentences.l: Do I seem now to owe heralds' praises to the deeds of your Hercules, o most beautiful commander of the Rhodian fleet?
sentences.i: So now do I look like a man who owes a herald's praise to your Hercules' deeds, most handsome captain of the Rhodian fleet?
sentences.n: praeconia are what a praeco, a public herald, cries out — formal, official praise; the question is whether Nestor owes any of it. tui and Herculis stand apart with praeconia rebus between them, “to the deeds of your Hercules”, and tui does the same work as tuus genitor did earlier: it keeps the man at arm's length. The sentence is a question only by Magnus's punctuation — there is no interrogative word in it. The elaborate vocative comes in the middle of a refusal to praise, and pulcherrime, “most beautiful”, is aimed at Tlepolemus himself rather than at anything he has done.

sentences.t:
Nec tamen ulterius, quam fortia facta silendo
ulciscor fratres: solida est mihi gratia tecum.”
sentences.l: Yet I avenge my brothers no further than by keeping silent about his brave deeds: the goodwill I have with you is solid.”
sentences.i: Still, I take my revenge for my brothers no further than by saying nothing of his brave deeds: the goodwill between you and me is unbroken.”
sentences.n: ulterius quam is “further than”, and the comparison is completed by silendo, an ablative gerund of means which keeps fortia facta as its object: silence is the whole of the revenge, and Nestor says so as a limit he has set himself. gratia here is the good standing between two people, not gratitude, and solida, “solid, unbroken”, says there is no crack in it: the grievance is against Hercules, not against Hercules' son.

sentences.t:
Haec postquam dulci Neleius edidit ore,
a sermone senis repetito munere Bacchi
surrexere toris: nox est data cetera somno.
sentences.l: After the Neleian had brought these things out with sweet mouth, away from the old man's talk, with the gift of Bacchus taken up again, they rose from the couches: the rest of the night was given to sleep.
sentences.i: When Neleus' son had brought all this out in that sweet voice of his, they turned from the old man's talk back to the gift of Bacchus, and then rose from the couches: what was left of the night was given over to sleep.
sentences.n: Ovid's own narration resumes here, after the closing quotation mark. postquam takes the perfect indicative edidit, “after he uttered”. Neleius is “the son of Neleus”, Nestor, named from his father as his brothers were at Nelidae. dulci ... ore is an ablative of manner. repetito munere Bacchi is an ablative absolute, “the gift of Bacchus having been taken up again” — wine is the god's gift, and the drinking resumes when the story stops. surrexere is surrexerunt, the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere; toris is ablative of separation, “from the couches”. cetera is separated from its noun nox by est data: “the rest of the night”.
